questions.question: Q1. In an Ashby materials map for 4D-active systems, what does the M_1 index represent?

answers.b: The bending stiffness per unit mass (√E / ρ).
answers.d: The time to shape memory recovery.

explanations.b: Correct - M₁ = √E/ρ is the specific stiffness, crucial for lightweight actuators.
explanations.c: Incorrect - That is M₂ = σ_recovery / ρ.
explanations.d: Incorrect - Recovery rate is not captured by any single index.

questions.question: Q2. Why must the three Ashby material performance indices (M₁, M₂, M₃) be normalized to [0,1]?

answers.a: Because they span many orders of magnitude and must be weighted fairly.
answers.b: To make all materials equally good.
answers.d: Because the lab requires dimensionless numbers.

explanations.a: Correct - Min-max normalization puts disparate properties (stiffness, stress, efficiency) on a common scale so weights matter equally.
explanations.b: Incorrect - Normalization reveals differences; it doesn't obscure them.
explanations.c: Incorrect - Simplicity alone is not the physics reason.
explanations.d: Incorrect - Dimensional analysis is separate from normalization strategy.

questions.question: Q3. The Timoshenko bilayer formula relates curvature κ to which of the following?

answers.a: Only the temperature of the material.
answers.c: Mismatch strain Δε, thickness ratio m, and modulus ratio n.

explanations.a: Incorrect - The Timoshenko model is strain-driven, not temperature-driven.
explanations.b: Incorrect - h enters the formula but is not the only factor.
explanations.c: Correct - κ = 6ΔE(1+m)²/(h·φ) couples strain mismatch with layer geometry and stiffness.
explanations.d: Incorrect - R_r is inherited from Exp 7 and enters Sub-Calc B separately.

questions.question: Q4. What is the shape error acceptance criterion in Sub-Calc B?

explanations.a: Incorrect - Too strict for finite strain simulations.
explanations.b: Correct - ε_shape = |κ_sim - κ_pred| / κ_pred × 100 % must stay below 10 % to ACCEPT.
explanations.c: Incorrect - Still tighter than the design gate.
explanations.d: Incorrect - Too loose; would admit poor geometries.

questions.question: Q5. In Sub-Calc C, why does a 4D part with a body-heat trigger (e.g., biomedical SMP at 37°C) always win on energy versus a moulded part with an active actuator?

answers.a: Because the moulding process is slow.
answers.d: Because body heat is free, so E_trigger ≈ 0 J/cycle, making the 4D energy line never catch the conventional line.

explanations.a: Incorrect - Speed of manufacture is not the energy advantage.
explanations.b: Incorrect - Material weight is accounted in the energy budget separately.
explanations.c: Incorrect - Renewability doesn't change the energy accounting.
explanations.d: Correct - When E_trigger < E_actuator, the 4D part wins at all cycle counts N, which is the compelling advantage in implantable medical devices.

questions.question: Q6. Sub-Calc C compares two energy curves: E_4D(N) and E_conv(N). What does N_break represent?

answers.a: The cycle count at which the two energy costs are equal.
answers.b: The maximum cycles the 4D part can survive.
answers.c: The minimum design life of the part.
answers.d: The number of cycles per second.

explanations.a: Correct - N_break is where E_4D(N) = E_conv(N); above it, moulding + actuator becomes cheaper per cycle.
explanations.b: Incorrect - That is fatigue life, not an economic crossover.
explanations.c: Incorrect - Design life and break-even cycle count are different quantities.
explanations.d: Incorrect - N is a count, not a rate.

questions.question: Q7. The print time for a 4D part scales with the volumetric FDM rate (≈ 4 mm³/s). This means the cost per part is _____ with production volume.

answers.d: rising with volume due to material scrap

explanations.a: Incorrect - Flatness is the defining feature of additive cost structure.
explanations.b: Incorrect - That is the injection-moulding curve.
explanations.c: Correct - Additive manufacturing has no tooling cost, so per-part cost depends only on print time and material, not on batch size.
explanations.d: Incorrect - FDM waste is nearly zero.

questions.question: Q8. When comparing 4D-printing cost to injection moulding cost across volume, the break-even volume N_break is determined by which quantity?

answers.d: The mould cost C_mould divided by the cost difference per part.

explanations.a: Incorrect - Material is one factor; tooling dominates moulding economics.
explanations.b: Incorrect - R_r is relevant to shape verification (Sub-Calc B), not manufacturing cost.
explanations.c: Incorrect - Print speed is embedded in C_4D but is not the single determinant.
explanations.d: Correct - N_break = C_mould / (C_4D - C_marginal); higher tooling pushes break-even to larger runs.

questions.question: Q9. According to the capstone, most 4D consumer goods remain at TRL 3 because they are blocked by which Sub-Calc gate?

answers.b: Sub-Calc D (manufacturing scalability and the cost break-even volume).

explanations.a: Incorrect - Material selection is not the scaling barrier.
explanations.b: Correct - Consumer goods lack the production volume to beat injection moulding on unit cost, so the technology stays at TRL 3 (analytical proof), not TRL 7+ (production-ready).
explanations.c: Incorrect - Energy is a niche advantage for biomedical, not mass-market.
explanations.d: Incorrect - Shape verification is TRL 4-5, not consumer-goods level.

questions.question: Q10. Why does the design review capstone inherit material properties (R_r from Exp 1, bilayer formula from Exp 2, bioprint window from Exp 7) rather than measure them fresh?

answers.a: Because the review is a capstone that closes the loop by synthesizing earlier decisions and showing how they interconnect in a real design.
answers.b: To save time and avoid redundant experiments.
answers.c: Because those experiments are more accurate.
answers.d: To test whether students read the earlier experiments.

explanations.a: Correct - The capstone's point is to show that earlier-experiment results form the building blocks of a complete design decision: material choice feeds shape verification, which feeds energy trade-offs, which feed scalability, ultimately to TRL placement.
explanations.c: Incorrect - Fresh measurement would be equally valid; inheritance is a pedagogical choice.
explanations.d: Incorrect - Synthesis, not testing, is the pedagogical goal.
